stem: Cotton’s importance to the Southern economy grew in this period mainly because

options.text: the federal government banned cotton imports
options.misconception: The United States exported cotton; no ban on cotton imports drove its growth.

options.text: the South had stopped growing all other crops besides cotton
options.misconception: The South still grew tobacco, rice, sugar, and food crops; cotton grew alongside them.

options.text: the cotton gin made short-staple cotton profitable, and British mills wanted it
slavery had been abolished in the border states by 1820 already
options.misconception: Slavery continued in the border states; its abolition there is not part of this story.

rationales.A: The United States sold cotton abroad, it did not buy it. A ban on imports cannot explain an export boom.
rationales.B: Tobacco, rice, and sugar stayed important Southern crops. Cotton grew fastest, but it did not replace the rest.
rationales.C: Whitney’s cotton gin cleaned short-staple cotton cheaply, so planters could grow it across the South, and British textile mills bought all they could. Supply and demand grew together.
rationales.D: Slavery was not abolished in the border states in this period. The cotton boom ran on enslaved labor, not on its end.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what changed on the supply side. The cotton gin made short-staple cotton cheap to clean.
2. Ask what changed on the demand side. British mills needed ever more raw cotton for their cloth.
3. Ask what tied them together. Planters with enslaved labor grew the fiber the mills wanted.
4. Put it together. A cheaper supply met a hungry market, and cotton became king.
Background: Eli Whitney’s cotton gin let Southern planters greatly increase cotton production, which fed the Industrial Revolution in Britain and the United States.
Remember: a boom usually needs both a supply change and a demand change, so look for both.
